Thanks for the call today, Maya — helpful context. A couple of follow-ups from our side as we scope the integration: 

- Our primary latency SLO is 200ms p95 for short chat flows (<=512 tokens output). For longer summarization jobs we can tolerate up to 1.2s p95 if throughput remains reasonable.
- Typical concurrency per service instance will be ~30 steady requests, but we spiky-burst up to 120 during morning batch runs.
- We stream partial outputs to the UI for chat; clients expect first tokens within 100ms for short queries.

Can you confirm whether Redwood can meet the 200ms p95 target at ~30 concurrent with streaming on a recommended model/quantization profile? Also attaching the sample transcript/usage patterns.

Cheers,

Anita — thanks for the clear notes and the usage file. Quick recap from our side + proposed next steps so we can validate with a short PoC: 

Summary:
- Short chat flow target: 200ms p95 (<=512 out). Streaming required (first token <=100ms).
- Long batch summarization: p95 tolerable up to 1.2s, but throughput target is 400 reqs/hour during peak windows.
- Concurrency: steady ~30, burst to ~120.

What we'll do next (PoC scope):
1) Run a dedicated perf pass with a candidate model family (open 7B-13B variants) under streaming + non-streaming modes.
2) Validate p95 latency at 30 and 120 concurrency points; measure first-token latency for streaming.
3) Produce a short matrix (latency/throughput vs token window and quantization) and a recommended fallback plan when >120 concurrent.

Ask: can you share a small set (5–10) of representative prompts for short-chat and 3 long summaries so we can reproduce token distributions?

I'll loop in Aditya (SE) for technical tuning and Laura for SRE/handoff. We aim to have initial numbers in 3 business days.

Hi Anita — looping details from today's SE review and what we'll test during the PoC. High-level technical notes: 

- Candidate models: we recommend starting with Redwood-13B-OPTq (quantized INT8 path) and Redwood-7B-Act (FP16) depending on fidelity needs. 13B-OPTq gives better throughput for streaming at slightly higher tail latency variance.
- Streaming first-token latency typically dominated by model warm-start + network; with prefix caching we can hit ~80–120ms first token p50 on a dedicated instance, p95 closer to 180–220ms depending on request alignment and batch aggregation windows.
- For 512-token outputs, 200ms p95 is achievable at low concurrency; at steady 30 concurrent we expect 220–350ms p95 unless we use aggressive batching and prefix caching.
- For burst to 120, we recommend a fallback routing policy: route new requests to a lower-capacity but lower-latency variant (7B FP16) or enable a short-term reserved burst pool (Dedicated) to preserve tail latency.

Planned measurements in PoC:
- First-token latency distribution (streaming) at concurrencies: 5, 30, 60, 120.
- Full-response p50/p95 for outputs of 64/256/512/1024 tokens.
- Token-per-second throughput and GPU utilization to estimate cost.

I'll attach a matrix (slo_scenarios.pdf) with the initial hypothesis. If Kestrel can accept a short warm-up (few minutes) and allow session affinity for chat users we can squeeze tail latencies down significantly.

Thanks,
Aditya Rao
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Ben and I are okay with a PoC that runs against our staging traffic shape (we'll mirror 30m of morning peak). Next: can we get a short test plan and exact API payload shape you need so we can mirror it? Also please include any specific headers for routing/fallback toggles.
